A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SafeDPO and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, ablations, human evaluations, three-seed results, and training-time measurements in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds XSTest evaluations, GPT-5.1 pairwise comparisons, and failure cases.

M1.justification: v1 Equation 13 retains pairs containing two unsafe responses; v2 Section 3.2 explicitly discards them. The preference-swapping rule and safety-margin loss otherwise remain substantially unchanged, while Section 3.4 adds a general SafeDAA recipe. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun under the revised filtering rule.

E1.justification: v2 adds XSTest, covering 250 benign and 200 unsafe prompts, including benign requests with misleading harmful-sounding wording. This substantially broadens evaluation beyond the retained PKU-SafeRLHF setting to test excessive refusal.

E2.justification: The original main and supplementary comparator sets are retained, including MoCAN and PeCAN. However, SACPO and P-SACPO participate in the added direct pairwise judge comparisons in v2 Table 22; they were absent from v1's pairwise win-rate tables, although already present in Figure 2.

E3.justification: v2 introduces GPT-5.1 judging for XSTest and defines over-refusal through partial or full refusals on benign prompts. Appendix D.2 adds direct SafeDPO-versus-baseline judgments and helpfulness evaluation restricted to pairs where both responses are safe. The original GPT-4 evaluations and human-study protocol are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a safety-controlled helpfulness analysis and investigates over-refusal through concrete failure cases, including benign software and household requests. Appendix E also examines benchmark-labeling limitations and a new judge-rationale example. The existing margin, model-scale, and evaluator-overoptimization studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions' Appendix C.7 and Table 13 report the same three-seed means and standard errors. The added evaluations introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice, significance tests, or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: Table 3 reports SafeDPO's 12.4% over-refusal and 100% harmless ratio on XSTest, while Table 23 reports a 59.66% helpfulness win rate against SafeRLHF among safe–safe pairs. These are new evaluations, not improvements over v1 under identical settings. The original plots and matched appendix result tables retain their findings and values.

T1.justification: Assumption 4.1 changes from requiring a lower probability bound for one safe response to bounding total safe-response probability. Proposition 4.3 becomes an objective-equality statement, and Appendices A.2–A.3 replace the earlier arguments with separate safety-pair cases incorporating discarded unsafe–unsafe pairs. These substantively revise the mathematical foundation; the finite-penalty convergence argument itself already existed in v1.

C1.justification: The central claims remain single-stage safety alignment without auxiliary reward/cost models or online sampling, an optimum-preserving safety margin, and competitive safety and helpfulness. v2 foregrounds closed-form optimality and scalability, but both were already claimed or demonstrated in v1.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive interpretation of over-refusal as a safety–permissiveness trade-off, proposes lexical-trigger explanations, questions some XSTest labels, and interprets the new safe–safe comparisons. Safety–helpfulness confounding was already discussed in v1. The original offline-applicability limitation and broader misuse/data-quality caveats are omitted.

D1.justification: The added evaluations document the GPT-5.1 judge, reused T2 template, and safe–safe selection procedure. Existing hardware, training hyperparameters, model identifiers, baseline checkpoint information, and human-participant instructions remain substantively unchanged.

R1.justification: v1's dedicated Related Works section is removed without an equivalent replacement. Detailed positioning against constrained alignment methods, Aligner, Metaaligner, and broader preference-learning research is substantially reduced, with many corresponding citations removed. v2 adds the XSTest reference and retains shorter discussions of the principal baselines.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, results discussion, conclusion, and much appendix prose are extensively rewritten. Theory becomes a separate main section, experiments gain a benchmark-based hierarchy, and appendix sections are reorganized. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 are redrawn with larger labels, markers, and legends. v2 adds XSTest and pairwise-comparison tables, tabulates Figure 2 values, and repeats existing model-scale and human-study tables in the main text. Numerous appendix tables and example displays are reformatted, including boxed instructions and prompts, alongside the conference-template layout change.

improvement.justification: XSTest and the safe–safe comparisons address v1's missing benign-prompt evaluation and acknowledged safety–helpfulness confounding, while failure examples make practical limitations clearer. These gains are tempered by lost related-work context and a new numerical inconsistency: Table 22's DPO-HARMLESS helpfulness win/tie/loss percentages total 109.01%. Overall, the revision provides a limited net quality improvement.
